The final model is refit on the full training set, and the process is repeated 100 times per model. The fold-count discrepancy is unresolved.

This process is repeated 100 times for each model.
Once the final tuning values are assigned, we refit the final model by using the entire training set.

review_notes: Selected the predictive-classifier family in section 7.1 because the paper title and abstract frame the study around predictive ability and out-of-sample attack prediction, and the authors explicitly choose among SVM, NN, and RF for that task. Retain the three main-specification (a) training classifiers in Table 8 Panel A, the RF importance output in Panel B, and the same flagged-user GRW holdout result in Table 9 column User. Exclude Table 8 RF^b because its note identifies it as a robustness specification; exclude Table 9 Exchange, Gambling, and Service group columns as additional business-type group applications; exclude the earlier event-study and Sri Lanka forensic case-study analyses as separate supporting empirical analyses rather than the selected predictive classifier family.

The introduction says the models are trained across all users and that the flagged user has the best training accuracy (physical p. 7); section 7.1 instead says the models are trained using the flagged user (physical p. 32). The detailed section 7.1 description and Table 9 identification of GRW are retained for the selected training/holdout description, but the training population remains unresolved.

Section 7.1 calls the procedure tenfold cross-validation, then says each round partitions training into 19 equally sized subsets; the fold count is unresolved. The Table 9 note independently says 10-fold cross-validation.

The paper reports 7,443,285 transfers for GRW, a roughly 70/30 observation split, and 21/9 attack events; it does not give exact training/validation row counts or fully reconcile transfer-user level predictors with the day-level Terror_t outcome. sample_size therefore remains null; the event counts are preserved as events, not observations.

The prose definition of Anonymous on physical p. 33 says transfers were to an anonymous address; the selected Table 8 note on p. 35 defines it as funds coming from or sent to an anonymous address. The selected table-note definition is retained, with the directional wording difference flagged.
results_review_notes: The extraction records classifier performance metrics and RF variable-importance scores as auxiliary/non-coefficient outcomes; the paper does not report ordinary coefficient estimates for SVM, NN, or RF.
For Table 8 Panel A, only main-specification columns SVM^a, NN^a, and RF^a are selected. RF^b is explicitly a robustness specification and is excluded.

Table 9 User is the held-out GRW result for the central out-of-sample predictive test. The Exchange, Gambling, and Service columns are group applications and are excluded from the selected baseline family.

Reported test p-values are retained exactly; unknown testing distributions are not inferred. Table 9 95% accuracy confidence interval endpoints are recorded as separate auxiliary bounds because the schema has no interval-valued estimate field.

Related Table 1 summaries are broader than the GRW classifier sample. No descriptive rows were found for Terror or the other model features In, Out, Anonymous, Exchange, Mixer, DarkMarkets, and Sigma; Table 1 does not report their classifier-level distribution. No descriptive N was inferred from the paper’s transfer totals or event counts.
